passage:
Shankar,
I'm leaving this in your maths notebook because you haven't answered my messages for a week, and I don't want to add more pings. I'm not angry. I can tell something's wrong, and I really don't know what it is. Maybe I did something dumb at the match. Maybe it's not about me at all. Either way, I'd honestly rather hear it, even if it's bad, than keep guessing. You don't have to write a long reply. You can just write "Tuesday after school" and I'll be at the tea stall. I'll listen first. I promise not to argue. And if it's something you can't say yet, that's okay too. I'll still be around.
Still your friend,
Madhav

qa.q: Where did Madhav leave the letter?
qa.a: Madhav left it in Shankar's maths notebook.

qa.q: What does Madhav want Shankar to feel when reading the letter?
qa.a: Madhav wants Shankar to feel safe rather than accused, so that speaking up feels easier than staying silent.

qa.q: Which parts of the letter make it easier for Shankar to reply?
qa.a: It says "I'm not angry", admits not knowing, offers a tiny way to reply ("Tuesday after school") and promises to listen first.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel finding this letter after a week of silence?
qa.a: Shankar may feel relieved and a little embarrassed, with an easy way back that doesn't require admitting fault. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen gently naming a friend's silence without accusation and inviting the truth, making speaking safer than staying quiet.

passage: "So I didn't know what to do," Sarika said, sitting cross-legged on the terrace with her cousin. "Irawati had gone totally silent. Eight days. And my first draft was awful: 'If you have a problem with me, just say it instead of acting like a baby.' I almost sent it. Then I thought, what would I want to get if I were her? So I deleted it and wrote, 'I can tell you're upset, and I honestly don't know why. I'd rather hear it, even if it's something I did.' That's it. No blaming. She read it at eleven at night. Nothing. Then at 11:40 she wrote, 'It was the Holi photo.' And we talked till one."

qa.q: What did Irawati say it was about?
qa.a: She wrote, "It was the Holi photo."

qa.q: Why did Sarika delete the first draft?
qa.a: Sarika imagined receiving it in Irawati's place and realised the hurtful accusation would only push Irawati, already upset, deeper into silence.

qa.q: What made the second message work?
qa.a: It named the upset without blaming, admitted not knowing, and invited the truth even if it was Sarika's fault.

qa.q: What might Irawati have felt in the forty minutes before she replied?
qa.a: She may have been torn between pride and relief, deciding whether it felt safe enough to speak.

grounding: Shows a teen replacing an accusing draft with a kind message that names the silence and invites the truth, which gets the friend talking.

passage:
I sit behind Hafsa in maths, so I saw it all. For almost a week, her best friend Jaspreet hadn't spoken to her. Not a word, not even a glance.
On Thursday, Hafsa wrote something on a page, tore it out carefully and folded it twice. She passed it forward at the end of the period.
Jaspreet opened it. I could read it over her shoulder, I admit. "I can tell you're upset and I don't know why. I'd rather hear it, even if it's bad. I won't get angry."
Jaspreet's shoulders came down. She read it again. Then she turned around and said, very quietly, "After school?"
I'm Harish, and I've never seen a note do that.

qa.q: How long had Jaspreet not spoken to Hafsa?
qa.a: For almost a week.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling while watching the note being passed?
qa.a: Harish was curious and then impressed, surprised at what a simple note could do.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa's note work?
qa.a: It named Jaspreet's upset kindly, invited her to speak and promised not to get angry, so speaking felt safer than staying silent.

qa.q: What was Jaspreet experiencing when she read the note?
qa.a: She seemed relieved; her shoulders came down, and she felt safe enough to suggest talking after school.

grounding: An observer sees a teenage girl send a kind note inviting her silent friend to speak, and the friend softens and agrees to talk.

passage:
Saturday: Gurleen had ignored Gargi's messages for six days. Gargi had tried "what's your problem?" and "fine, be like that." Nothing.
Sunday: Gargi sat on the stairs of her building, thinking. Accusing her wasn't working. Maybe Gurleen was scared, not just angry. She typed slowly: "I can feel you're upset with me and I don't know why. I'd rather hear it, even if it's hard. I'm listening." She read it five times before sending.
Tuesday: Gurleen came to her desk before assembly. "Can we talk at break?" At break, Gurleen said, "I didn't think you'd want to hear it." "I do," said Gargi. And Gurleen finally told her.

qa.q: How many days had Gurleen ignored Gargi's messages?
qa.a: Six days.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as she read her message five times before sending?
qa.a: She felt nervous and hopeful, wanting to reach Gurleen without accusing her.

qa.q: What changed between Saturday and Sunday that helped?
qa.a: Gargi stopped accusing and instead sent a kind invitation, naming the upset without blame and saying she'd rather hear it.

qa.q: What was Gurleen experiencing before Tuesday?
qa.a: She was hurt and also afraid that Gargi wouldn't want to hear what was wrong.

grounding: Over a few days, a teenager swaps accusations for a kind invitation to speak, and the silent friend feels safe enough to talk.

passage:
Madhuri, you look like a girl whose friend has stopped talking to her. Come, I'll tell you what I did at fifteen. I'm your Dolma Aunty, and I learned this the hard way.
My friend Sonam went silent for a whole week. I tried shouting. I tried ignoring her back. Nothing worked.
Then my mother said, "Ask her, but make it safe." So I wrote on a small card: "I can see you are upset and I don't know what I did. I want to hear it, even if it's bad."
I slipped it into her book. The next morning she was waiting for me at the gate. She said, "You really want to know?"
That card saved our friendship. We're still friends, forty years on.

qa.q: Where did Dolma put the card?
qa.a: She slipped it into Sonam's book.

qa.q: What was young Dolma feeling after shouting and ignoring didn't work?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and helpless, having tried everything with no result.

qa.q: In the story, what was the choice that turned things around?
qa.a: Following her mother's advice, young Dolma wrote a card that invited Sonam to speak without accusing her, which made talking safer than silence.

qa.q: What was Sonam going through when she waited at the gate?
qa.a: She was likely nervous and a bit hopeful, checking whether Dolma really wanted to hear her hurt.

grounding: An aunt recalls sending a friend a kind card inviting her to say what was wrong, which ended the silence by making speaking feel safe.

passage:
Dhruv had one bar of signal on the roof of his grandmother's house in Kangra, and a data pack that was almost gone.

For five days, Gurpreet hadn't replied. Not in class before the holidays, not now. The old Dhruv would have sent, "What's your problem??" He'd typed it twice and deleted it.

The signal flickered. He had maybe one message left before the pack ran out. He wrote it slowly, standing on tiptoe by the water tank:

"I can tell you're upset with me and I honestly don't know why. I'd rather hear it, even if it's bad. I'm not angry. Just miss you."

He pressed send. The bar vanished. He stood in the wind for a long time, watching the valley go dark.

The next morning his grandmother's phone rang. It was Gurpreet, asking for him.

qa.q: Where was Dhruv staying?
qa.a: He was at his grandmother's house in Kangra.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he stood watching the valley after sending the message?
qa.a: He felt anxious and hopeful, unsure whether the message had arrived or whether Gurpreet would answer.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv's message work better than 'What's your problem??'?
qa.a: It invited Gurpreet to speak without accusation and said he wasn't angry, which made talking feel safer than staying silent.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt reading Dhruv's message?
qa.a: Gurpreet probably felt relieved and less defensive, since the message showed care rather than blame.

grounding: With a failing signal, a teen sends a gentle message naming the silence without accusing, making it safer to talk.
